status: PROPOSAL - research data only. This file is NOT authoritative simulation state and NOT renderer presentation data. It does not finalise a runtime schema. Canonical settlement/location identities (RFC 4122 UUIDv5, ADR-0009) are minted only by the atlas pipeline at integration time; the proposedId values here are research handles, not canonical IDs.
subject: R-16 historical settlement roster, second batch (batch 2)
envelopeRegions: 7 - Greece, the Aegean & Crete (mid ~92); 8 - Anatolia & the Black Sea (mid ~80)
batchScope: Mainland Greece (Peloponnese, central Greece, Thessaly, Epirus, Aetolia and the Euboean gulf), the Aegean islands and Crete, and western Anatolia with the western Black-Sea coast
coordinateConvention: WGS84 decimal degrees, approximate representative points for the ancient site (not the modern town unless noted). Precision does not imply archaeological accuracy and is not a surveyed building location.
idScheme: proposedId = r16-gre-<slug> for Greece/Aegean/Crete (envelope region 7) or r16-ana-<slug> for Anatolia/Black Sea (envelope region 8); the slug (key) is region-scoped to avoid homonyms. Stable, human-readable, non-canonical.
methodNote: Records are compiled from independent evidence (primary literary/administrative sources, archaeology and the Pleiades gazetteer for coordinates). Game/mod faction names are discovery leads only and never authorities. Every coordinate is a representative point with an explicit location confidence; where only a broad location is known the coordinate is coarse or null. Political authority is recorded only where supported; otherwise it is left unclaimed.
sourceAuditNote: Pleiades gazetteer identifiers are recorded only as 'to be confirmed', never asserted: automated access to pleiades.stoa.org was blocked by the site's anti-scraping protection during this pass, so no Pleiades id has been verified. Coordinates are approximate representative points, not surveyed locations. The Hellenistic literary sources (Polybius, Livy, Diodorus, Pausanias, Strabo, Plutarch, Justin, Arrian) are later than 278 BCE and are dated in each record. The 278 horizon is one of acute political flux (the Gallic invasion, the collapse of Lysimachus' kingdom, Antigonus Gonatas not yet king, Pyrrhus in the west); later political control must NOT be retrojected. Confirming Pleiades ids and coordinates manually remains an integration prerequisite.
politicalContext278Bce: The Gallic (Galatian) invasion is in progress (Delphi 279; Lysimachia 277). Macedon is in chaos: Ptolemy Keraunos killed 279, Antigonus Gonatas not yet recognised king (king 276/275 after his 277 victory). Byzantium and the N. Aegean are pressured. Aetolia is strong and holds Delphi. The Achaean League was only just revived (c.281/280) by four cities. Athens is free but its Piraeus is garrisoned. In Anatolia the Seleucid Antiochus I holds the interior, Philetaerus rules Pergamon as a Seleucid-nominal dynast, Ptolemy II holds or influences coastal bases, Bithynia is under Zipoetes (d.278), and the Galatians are crossing into Anatolia (278/277).
duplicateGuard: None of these records reproduce the 23 active atlas sites, the 12 deferred atlas candidates, the excluded site (Cosa), or any of the 55 batch-1 central-Mediterranean records. The id prefixes r16-gre- and r16-ana- are disjoint from r16-ita-.

records.existenceEvidence: A major Dorian polis on the Isthmus controlling the land route between the Peloponnese and central Greece, with the ports of Lechaeum and Cenchreae; one of the enduring Greek cities.
records.politicalAuthority: Greek polis under an Antigonid (Macedonian) garrison holding Acrocorinth (a 'fetter of Greece'); exact 278 tenure is debated but Antigonid control is probable.
records.architectureContext: Twin-harbour city at the Isthmus with the fortified acropolis of Acrocorinth and the sanctuary of Poseidon at Isthmia; Doric temple remains.
chronologyNotes: Macedonian (Antigonid) garrison on Acrocorinth in this period.
Roman sack 146 BCE and Roman colony 44 BCE are far later.
anachronismWarnings: Do NOT show the Roman colony (Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis, 44 BCE) or the 146 BCE destruction.
Do not show the later Roman forum/monumentality.
sources: Pleiades gazetteer (record id to be confirmed)
unresolved: Whether the garrison was Antigonid or another power (e.g. Ptolemaic) in the campaign year.

records.existenceEvidence: A leading Argolid polis with the Heraion and a long civic history; a substantial city through the early Hellenistic period.
records.politicalAuthority: Greek polis; generally aligned with Macedon in this period (Antigonid influence), exact status uncertain.
records.architectureContext: Walled city with the extramural Heraion and the Aspis citadel; theatre and agora.
chronologyNotes: Hellenistic Argos under shifting Macedonian and local dynasts.
anachronismWarnings: Do not show the later Roman colony or imperial monuments.
sources: Pleiades gazetteer (record id to be confirmed)
unresolved: Precise 278 factional control (pro-Macedonian vs independent).

records.existenceEvidence: The leading Laconia n polis, capital of the Lakedaimonian state and seat of the dual kingship; an independent power in the early 3rd c. under king Areus I.
records.politicalAuthority: Independent Lakedaimonian kingdom (dual kingship; Agiad king Areus I, 309-265).
records.architectureContext: Unwalled in the classical manner until the fortifications of c.294; a sanctuary-rich, sprawling settlement of villages rather than a single dense walled town.
chronologyNotes: Areus I ruling; period of attempted reform and Ptolemaic/Antigonid alignments.
anachronismWarnings: Do not show Roman Sparta or the later theatre/monumental development.
sources: Pleiades gazetteer (record id to be confirmed)

records.existenceEvidence: The great Arcadian city founded in 371 as a counterweight to Sparta; a major regional centre with an extensive wall circuit and a famous theatre.
records.politicalAuthority: Independent Arcadian polis with Macedonian (Antigonid) alignment in this period (probable).
records.architectureContext: Very large walled city on the Megalopolis plain, with the Thersilion assembly hall and a large theatre; strategically barring Laconia.
chronologyNotes: Founding 371; early Hellenistic dynamism; later joins the Achaean League (2nd half of the 3rd c.).
anachronismWarnings: Do not show the later Achaean League or Roman reduction.
sources: Polybius, Histories (later; Polybius was a citizen)
Pleiades gazetteer (record id to be confirmed)
unresolved: Exact 278 internal regime (democracy vs tyrant) and alignment.

records.existenceEvidence: The city founded in 369 after the liberation of Messenia; protected by one of the finest surviving Greek circuit walls with the citadel of Ithome.
records.politicalAuthority: Independent Greek polis (Messenia).
records.architectureContext: Massive ashlar fortification circuit (largely extant) enclosing the city with the sanctuary of Asclepius and the Ithome acropolis.
chronologyNotes: Founding 369; independent poleis through the early Hellenistic period.
anachronismWarnings: Do not show Roman or later medieval Messene.
sources: Pleiades gazetteer (record id to be confirmed)

records.existenceEvidence: An Arcadian polis, site of the great battle of 362; the city was destroyed and resettled in the 220s but existed in the 278 horizon.
records.politicalAuthority: Independent Arcadian polis; later renamed Antigoneia under Macedonian influence (after the campaign date).
records.architectureContext: Walled plain city with a circuit wall and agora; rebuilt plan.
chronologyNotes: Battle of Mantinea 362; destroyed 223, after the campaign.
anachronismWarnings: Do not confuse with Antigoneia / the later refoundation.
sources: Pleiades gazetteer (record id to be confirmed)

records.existenceEvidence: A major Arcadian polis with the celebrated sanctuary of Athena Alea; occupied through the early Hellenistic period.
records.politicalAuthority: Independent Arcadian polis (later Achaean).
records.architectureContext: Walled city on the Tegea plain with the sanctuary of Athena Alea (the later classical temple).
chronologyNotes: Alea sanctuary long-standing; city active in the 3rd c.

records.architectureContext: Walled city on a plateau above the Asopus plain, controlling the approach to the gulf of Corinth.

records.existenceEvidence: The Eleian polis that administered the sanctuary and games of Zeus at Olympia; a substantial regional power in the north-west Peloponnese.

records.existenceEvidence: A leading Achaean polis that would become the league's federal meeting place; Polybius records that, about five years after the league's revival, Aegium expelled its foreign garrison and joined (i.e. c.276).
records.politicalAuthority: Achaean polis still under a foreign (Macedonian) garrison at 278; joins the league c.276.
records.architectureContext: Coastal city with the sanctuary of Zeus Homarius and a harbour; later the league's federal seat.
chronologyNotes: Polybius (2.41): Aegium joined about five years after the c.281/280 revival - so at 278 the garrison is still present.
anachronismWarnings: Do not present Aegium as the league seat at 278; that role develops later.
sources: Pleiades gazetteer (record id to be confirmed)

records.politicalAuthority: Independent Greek polis (Argolid).
records.architectureContext: City with the extramural Asclepieion (sanctuary, tholos and temple), above a small coastal plain.

records.existenceEvidence: The inland capital of the Epirote kingdom and the seat of Pyrrhus, on the river Arachthus; a substantial royal city.
records.politicalAuthority: Epirote (Molossian) royal capital under Pyrrhus' Aiakid dynasty.
records.architectureContext: Walled royal capital with a palace area, agora and the sanctuary of Apollo; the Arachthus and gulf give it a maritime outlet.

records.politicalAuthority: Sanctuary within the Epirote (Molossian) kingdom.

records.existenceEvidence: A major Ionian island polis with a naval tradition and a fine harbour, long contested between powers at the entrance to the Adriatic.

records.architectureContext: Walled port city on the east coast of the island, controlling the Corfu channel.

records.existenceEvidence: The panhellenic sanctuary and oracle of Apollo, attacked by the Gauls under Brennus in 279 and a central religious authority of the Greek world.
records.politicalAuthority: Sanctuary under the control of the Aetolian League (the Aetolians dominated the Amphictyony after the Gallic attack of 279).
records.architectureContext: Terraced sanctuary with the temple of Apollo, treasury buildings and the stadium; the site is a settlement as well as a sanctuary.

anachronismWarnings: Do not show the later Roman remodelling.

records.existenceEvidence: A naval port commanding the narrows of the gulf of Corinth; the Aetolians extended their membership to the Naupactians in the late 4th/early 3rd c., making it an Aetolian stronghold.

records.architectureContext: Walled harbour town on the north shore of the gulf of Corinth's entrance, with an acropolis.

records.existenceEvidence: The federal sanctuary of the Aetolian League, seat of its religious festivals and the repository of its records.

records.existenceEvidence: The foremost cultural and civic centre of the Greek world, with its democracy restored in 287 after the expulsion of the Macedonian garrison from the city; one of the largest cities of Greece.
records.politicalAuthority: Independent (free) polis with a restored democracy; Ptolemaic-aligned. The Piraeus, however, remained under a Macedonian garrison.
records.architectureContext: Walled city around the Acropolis with the agora, the classical temples and the Pnyx; the Long Walls link it to the Piraeus.
chronologyNotes: City freed 287 (garrison expelled); democracy restored.
Chremonidean War and the loss of independence come later (267-261).
anachronismWarnings: Do not show the later Roman/Hadrianic Athens.
Do not show the Chremonidean-War occupation or later garrisons.

records.existenceEvidence: The harbour town of Athens with its three harbours (Cantharos, Zea, Munychia); a major naval and commercial port.
records.politicalAuthority: The port/deme of Athens, but held by a Macedonian garrison in this period and thus politically separated from the free city.
records.architectureContext: Fortified harbour complex with ship-sheds, the Eetioneia and Munychia defences, and the asty linked by the Long Walls.
chronologyNotes: Macedonian garrison held the Piraeus while the city was free (a recurrent 3rd-c. situation).
anachronismWarnings: Do not show the later Roman or modern port.

records.existenceEvidence: The chief Boeotian city, destroyed by Alexander in 335 and rebuilt by Cassander from 316; a functioning city and seat of the Boeotian League by the early 3rd c.

records.architectureContext: Rebuilt circuit wall around the Kadmeia and lower town, with the Cadmean acropolis; a newly re-established urban fabric.

records.existenceEvidence: A first-rank commercial and naval power, victor of the great siege of 305/304, with a celebrated merchant marine and the three Rhodian cities unified into one state.

records.politicalAuthority: Greek polis whose sovereignty was contested between the Seleucid and Ptolemaic powers in this period; Ptolemaic influence is probable by the 270s-260s.
